title: SR&ED Direct Support Work | Canada FAQ
description: For Canadian SR&ED claimants, direct support work qualifies under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act. See when it counts.
summary: For Canadian SR&ED claimants, direct support work qualifies under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act when engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing or psychological research is commensurate with the needs of, and directly supports, basic research, applied research or experimental development in Canada, making otherwise routine tasks eligible.

body.text: For Canadian SR&ED claimants, direct support work qualifies under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act when engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing or psychological research is commensurate with the needs of, and directly supports, basic research, applied research or experimental development in Canada, making otherwise routine tasks eligible.
Executive and Legislative Landscape of Canadian Research and Development Incentives

Canada maintains one of the most mature and financially expansive statutory frameworks for industrial research and development among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) jurisdictions. The cornerstone of this fiscal architecture is the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program, which is jointly governed by the Department of Finance Canada—responsible for statutory policy design and legislative drafting—and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical eligibility reviews, financial compliance audits, and tax credit disbursements. Structured as a statutory entitlement under the Income Tax Act rather than a discretionary ministerial grant, the SR&ED program provides predictable, non-dilutive capital to between 19,000 and 24,160 corporate and unincorporated claimants annually across more than 22,000 processed claims. During the 2024–2025 fiscal year, the program delivered $4.5 billion in federal investment tax credits (ITCs), and for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, total federal SR&ED ITCs claimed reached $4.9 billion, with $4.6 billion formally allowed by the CRA. This trajectory represents an expansion of approximately 50% in annual credit value since fiscal 2022, underscoring the program's role as the primary fiscal pillar of Canadian industrial innovation policy.

The federal statutory mechanism operates through a dual-pillar incentive structure codified in the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR"). First, under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current expenditures—and, following recent legislative restoration, eligible capital expenditures—incurred in Canada for SR&ED. This pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures may be deducted in full against business income in the taxation year incurred, reducing current corporate tax liabilities, or carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years when the enterprise achieves commercial profitability. Second, under sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA, taxpayers earn federal ITCs calculated as a statutory percentage of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at year-end as defined in subsection 127(9). Depending on the legal status, ownership structure, size, and expenditure composition of the claimant, these ITCs either reduce Part I federal income tax payable or are paid out directly to the taxpayer as cash refunds under section 127.1.
The 2025–2026 Legislative Overhaul: Enactment of Bill C-15

Between 2024 and 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most consequential statutory expansion in more than a decade following two stages of Department of Finance public consultations aimed at reversing declining Canadian business R&D intensity, addressing capital flight in hardware-intensive sectors, and promoting domestic intellectual property retention. While initial consultation proposals in 2024 had contemplated an intermediate increase in the enhanced expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, the federal government subsequently expanded the reform package in Budget 2025. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, formally enacting the 2025–2026 SR&ED legislative enhancements into law.

The enacted amendments in Bill C-15 apply retroactively to taxation years that begin on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024), while the restoration of capital expenditure eligibility applies to depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and lease costs that first become payable on or after that date. This legislative overhaul transforms corporate R&D tax planning across five interconnected dimensions. First, the annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) has doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for qualifying corporations, increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Second, to prevent scaling mid-sized companies from prematurely phasing out of the 35% enhanced rate upon raising institutional venture capital or expanding production facilities, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out corridor was widened from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000.

Third, Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) may now elect to have their enhanced expenditure limit phase-out determined using a three-year average gross revenue calculation rather than taxable capital employed in Canada. This structural election eliminates a persistent distortion whereby pre-revenue or low-revenue biotechnology, clean technology, and hardware firms that accumulated substantial balance-sheet equity or debt to fund multi-year R&D cycles were previously penalized under the taxable capital test before generating commercial sales. Fourth, reversing a longstanding statutory restriction that confined the 35% refundable credit exclusively to private corporations, Bill C-15 extends access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC (up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit) to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), whose phase-out is mandatorily governed by the three-year average consolidated gross revenue test. Fifth, reversing the 2012 federal budget repeal (which had taken effect on January 1, 2014), Bill C-15 restores paragraph 37(1)(b) and amends subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III), subsection 127(9), subsection 127(11.5), and section 127.1 to reinstate capital property and related lease expenditures into both the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes. This restoration directly lowers the after-tax cost of R&D infrastructure for hardware-intensive enterprises, advanced manufacturing, life sciences, clean technology, and artificial intelligence firms acquiring graphics processing units (GPUs) and specialized compute clusters.

body.text: Statutory Definition of Eligible Activities and the Evolution of CRA Administrative Doctrine
The Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

Eligibility for both the subsection 37(1) expenditure deduction and the subsection 127(9) investment tax credit depends entirely on whether the underlying technical activities satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and classifies qualifying work into three primary substantive branches alongside one derivative support branch. The first branch, basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a), encompasses experimental or theoretical work undertaken primarily for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. The second branch, applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b), covers original investigation undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and commercially predominant branch, experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

In addition to these three core categories, paragraph 248(1)(d) extends statutory eligibility to support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight enumerated activities—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Consequently, routine computer programming or standard mechanical testing that would fail to qualify as standalone experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) becomes fully eligible under paragraph 248(1)(d) if it is strictly required to construct a test rig or execute an experiment designed to resolve an underlying technological uncertainty. Conversely, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes from the definition of SR&ED any work with respect to market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; or routine data collection.
The CRA's Two-Question ("Why" and "How") Eligibility Doctrine

In August 2021, the CRA archived its legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (along with numerous sector-specific application policy papers) and consolidated its administrative doctrine into the unified Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. Although the Federal Court of Appeal and the Tax Court of Canada have repeatedly affirmed that administrative guidelines cannot alter the statutory meaning of subsection 248(1) as established by judicial precedent, the CRA's Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) evaluate every project through a structured two-part inquiry framed around "Why" the work was conducted and "How" it was executed.

The first requirement—the "Why" inquiry—asks whether the work was conducted in order to advance scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. Under CRA doctrine and settled case law, a technological advancement cannot be achieved through the application of standard practice or "routine engineering," which encompasses techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Instead, a project must confront a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty: a fundamental limitation in the underlying stock of scientific knowledge or a system-level technological constraint, architectural conflict, or material incompatibility where it cannot be determined ex ante, based on publicly available knowledge and standard professional experience, whether the objective can be achieved at all or what technical avenue will resolve the impediment.

The second requirement—the "How" inquiry—asks whether the work was conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology through experiment or analysis. Being confronted with an uncertain path toward a technical objective is not, by itself, sufficient to qualify a project as SR&ED. The claimant must demonstrate that the uncertainty was investigated by qualified personnel following a disciplined scientific methodology comprising four sequential operational steps. First, the team must formulate a specific hypothesis—an idea consistent with known scientific or engineering facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the problem, articulated as a proposed causal relationship, structural design method, or algorithmic architecture. Second, the team must subject that hypothesis to rigorous testing by means of controlled experiment or analysis, recognizing that hypotheses frequently evolve or require modification across iterative cycles as initial trials fail or expose unanticipated boundary conditions. Third, the team must develop logical conclusions grounded in the quantitative or qualitative empirical findings generated by the experiments or analyses. Fourth, the claimant must maintain contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses to substantiate the hypotheses formulated, the experimental variables tested, and the resulting advancements in technological knowledge.
Sector-Specific Application: Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, and Hardware Systems

The boundary between routine engineering and qualifying experimental development is most intensely scrutinized by the CRA in software engineering and artificial intelligence claims. Deploying or fine-tuning off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) using standard vendor documentation, integrating third-party application programming interfaces (APIs), resolving syntax or software integration bugs, migrating legacy codebases to cloud infrastructure, or building complex commercial user interfaces constitutes routine software engineering and is ineligible for federal SR&ED tax credits—even when the resulting commercial software product is first-to-market or commercially innovative.

By contrast, software engineering and artificial intelligence development satisfies subsection 248(1) when development teams encounter fundamental algorithmic, architectural, or computational bottlenecks that cannot be resolved using documented computer science methodologies. Qualifying experimental development in software and AI typically arises when engineers must design novel model compression, quantization, or pruning algorithms to execute complex neural network inference within strict edge-device memory and latency envelopes where standard quantization degrades model accuracy below operational thresholds. Similarly, eligibility is established when teams conduct systematic experimentation to resolve distributed consensus, concurrency, or real-time state-synchronization failures under extreme throughput conditions where established database architectures exhibit non-linear latency spikes, or when they develop novel feature-extraction and synthetic training architectures to overcome sparse, noisy, or non-stationary physical sensor data in autonomous robotics, medical diagnostics, or industrial control systems. Furthermore, following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, AI, robotics, cleantech, and deep-tech firms conducting experimental development on or after December 16, 2024, can once again claim the acquisition or leasing of dedicated GPU clusters, high-performance compute infrastructure, and specialized laboratory testing apparatus as eligible capital or lease expenditures.
Judicial Precedents and Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence

Because the Income Tax Act does not statutorily define foundational concepts such as "technological advancement," "technological uncertainty," "hypothesis," or "routine engineering," Canadian courts have developed an extensive body of jurisprudence to adjudicate disputes between taxpayers and the Minister of National Revenue.
Foundational Interpretive and Analytical Precedents
Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 DTC 724 (TCC)

In Consoltex, Judge Bowman established the overarching canon of statutory construction governing SR&ED litigation in Canada. Recognizing that Parliament enacted the SR&ED provisions as a deliberate fiscal incentive to encourage industrial scientific research in Canada, the Tax Court of Canada held that the legislation must not be given a narrow, technical, or pedantic construction that defeats its parliamentary purpose, but rather "such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects". Subsequent decisions—including Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998) and Buehler Versatile Inc. v. The King (2023)—consistently invoke Consoltex to restrain overly rigid administrative denials by CRA auditors, while maintaining that the taxpayer bears the civil burden of proving eligibility on a balance of probabilities.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC)

Decided in May 1998 by Judge (later Chief Justice) Bowman, Northwest Hydraulic remains the foundational judicial authority in Canadian SR&ED law. Evaluating complex physical hydraulic scale modelling conducted by an engineering consultancy to solve non-linear fluid dynamics and sediment transport problems in river and dam structures, Judge Bowman distilled the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) into the seminal Five-Question Test. First, the Court asked whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Judge Bowman defined "routine engineering" as techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, and famously held that technological uncertainty is something that "exists in the mind of the specialist": if the resolution of a technical problem is not reasonably predictable using established engineering procedures, technological uncertainty exists even if the individual physical laws or equations are known.

Second, the Court asked whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Judge Bowman explained that this entails a five-stage methodological progression comprising the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear objective, the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate that uncertainty, and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. Third, the Court asked whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses, requiring systematic analytical rigour rather than intuitive trial-and-error. Fourth, the Court asked whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, which Judge Bowman characterized as an advancement in general understanding within the relevant engineering or scientific community. Crucially, proving scientifically why a hypothesized technical approach fails constitutes a valid technological advancement; commercial or technical failure of a prototype does not disqualify a project. Fifth, the Court asked whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA)

In C.W. Agencies, the Federal Court of Appeal formally endorsed and adopted Judge Bowman's five-question framework from Northwest Hydraulic at paragraph 17 of its judgment, elevating the five criteria to binding appellate precedent across all Canadian courts. Subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence—including Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205 (at paragraph 37) and Clevor Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 166 (at paragraph 11)—has confirmed that the five-factor test is strictly cumulative: to qualify as SR&ED under subsection 248(1), each of the five questions must be answered in the affirmative.
Contemporary Jurisprudence on Routine Engineering, Software, and Evidentiary Standards
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (FCA) and 2014 TCC 313 (Justice Jorré)

A recurring dispute during CRA audits and Tax Court litigation concerns the fifth question of Northwest Hydraulic: whether the absence of formal written contemporaneous records automatically invalidates an SR&ED claim as a matter of law. In RIS-Christie (at paragraphs 14–15) and subsequently in 2014 TCC 313 (at paragraph 94, Justice Jorré), the courts clarified that although contemporaneous documentation is frequently necessary in practice to resolve factual disputes between the taxpayer and the Minister, "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development". While credible, detailed oral testimony corroborated by indirect project artifacts is legally admissible to establish systematic experimentation, relying on oral memory without written experimental records exposes the claimant to severe litigation risk.
Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 DTC 1089 (TCC)

In Hypercube, Associate Chief Justice Lamarre dismissed an informal procedure appeal concerning $28,800 in software developer wages claimed for building an automated computer software program capable of inspecting and verifying websites. The corporate taxpayer contended that its development activities formed an integrated series of tasks required to achieve a technological advancement and argued that the CRA auditor had improperly divided the project into isolated subprojects to dismiss them as standard programming. Applying C.W. Agencies, the Tax Court held that resolving discrete programming problems within the known constraints of existing languages and frameworks constituted normal analyses carried out by competent programmers using current technology rather than SR&ED. Furthermore, the Court noted fatal evidentiary gaps in the taxpayer's employee time logs, which recorded hours for only one developer without linking specific coding iterations to the testing of scientific hypotheses.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (TCC)

Justice Sommerfeldt's decision in Joel Theatrical Rigging provides the most rigorous judicial analysis of "routine engineering," "hypothesis," and the "scientific method" in modern Tax Court jurisprudence. The taxpayer designed custom theatrical stage-rigging mechanisms and argued that bespoke engineering encountered unique structural uncertainties. In dismissing the appeal, Justice Sommerfeldt established three enduring legal standards. At paragraph 17, while acknowledging that there is no exhaustive statutory definition of "routine engineering," he held that even when a mechanical design is custom-built, complex, or novel, it remains routine engineering if the underlying structural or mechanical uncertainties can be resolved by applying established engineering principles, reference manuals, and mathematical formulas accessible to competent specialists. At paragraph 26, after surveying scientific and legal authorities, Justice Sommerfeldt concluded that a "hypothesis" under Question 2 of Northwest Hydraulic must be an explicit, testable statement proposing a causal mechanism or technical solution that is subsequently subjected to experiment or trial—not merely a commercial objective or design specification. Finally, at paragraph 33, he held that satisfying Question 3 requires procedures that accord with objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by systematic observation, hypothesis formulation, controlled testing where variables are isolated, and logical modification of hypotheses based on empirical test results.
National R & D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (TCC) and Zeuter Development Corp. v. The Queen (2021)

In National R & D, Justice Lafleur dismissed a general procedure appeal involving software development on the appellant's "PTS Project". While acknowledging per RIS-Christie and 2014 TCC 313 that oral testimony regarding contemporaneous coding notes taken by the lead developer was legally admissible, the Court found that the evidence failed to demonstrate that the coding work followed a systematic scientific investigation aimed at overcoming technological uncertainty rather than standard iterative software development. Similarly, in Zeuter Development Corp. v. The Queen (2021), the Tax Court denied SR&ED claims where the claimant failed to produce reliable contemporaneous records substantiating the formulation and testing of hypotheses as the work progressed.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (TCC, 2025)

Contrasting sharply with taxpayer defeats in poorly documented software and custom-fabrication appeals, the Tax Court's decision in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. (adjudicated by Justice Bodie regarding the 2020 taxation year) demonstrates how small and medium-sized enterprises can prevail against the Minister when all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are methodically proven. The appellant sought to develop a cold-pressed, vinegar-based carbonated juice beverage ("Chrisoda") capable of remaining shelf-stable at room temperature for at least two years without artificial chemical preservatives or thermal pasteurization that degraded flavour. Initial production runs suffered from unexpected microbial fermentation and exploding cans.

The Minister disallowed the SR&ED claim, asserting that the appellant merely utilized preservatives known to competent food scientists, failed to undertake a systematic investigation, and lacked adequate records. Justice Bodie overturned the reassessment and allowed the appeal in full. On Question 1, the Court held that while individual natural preservatives were known in food science, their behaviour and microbial inhibition thresholds within an unpasteurized, cold-pressed carbonated beverage matrix aiming for a two-year ambient shelf life presented a genuine technological uncertainty that could not be resolved through routine food-engineering procedures. On Questions 2, 3, and 4, applying Justice Sommerfeldt's framework from Joel Theatrical Rigging, Justice Bodie found that the appellant formulated explicit, testable hypotheses regarding microbial stabilization, conducted methodical multi-batch experiments isolating specific formulation parameters, and achieved a technological advancement that solved the can-explosion failure mode. On Question 5, the Court ruled that the appellant's batch records and laboratory test logs provided sufficient contemporaneous documentation of the hypotheses tested and results obtained as the work progressed.

body.text: Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Corporate Thresholds, and Phase-Out Mechanics

The quantum and cash refundability of federal SR&ED investment tax credits under sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act are governed by the claimant's corporate classification, associated corporate group structure, prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, and consolidated gross revenue.
The Enhanced 35% Refundable Credit for CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Under subsection 127(10.1) and section 127.1 of the ITA, as amended by Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, two distinct categories of Canadian corporations qualify for the enhanced 35% investment tax credit rate on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures per taxation year for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. The first category comprises Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), defined in subsection 125(7) and subsection 248(1) of the ITA as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than a corporation controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by one or more corporations whose shares are listed on a designated foreign stock exchange, or by any combination of them.

The second category comprises Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), newly created by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. An ECPC is a corporation resident in Canada whose shares are listed on a designated stock exchange (or that has elected to be a public corporation), provided it is not controlled directly or indirectly by non-resident persons and satisfies the statutory gross revenue thresholds. Extending the 35% refundable credit to ECPCs removes a major structural impediment in Canadian capital markets—often termed the "IPO cliff"—whereby high-growth Canadian biotechnology, clean technology, hardware, and software companies previously forfeited the 35% refundable SR&ED rate and dropped immediately to the 15% non-refundable rate upon listing on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) or TSX Venture Exchange (TSXV).
Mathematical Mechanics of the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

The maximum $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit must be shared and formally allocated among all associated corporations within a corporate group using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated to reflect the $6,000,000 cap under subsection 127(10.6)).

For CCPCs applying the default Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula in taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 raised the phase-out corridor from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, calculated on an associated-group basis under Part I.3 of the ITA. Under amended subsection 127(10.2), the corporation's annual expenditure limit is governed by the statutory formula:

In this statutory expression, the variable A is nil where prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less and, in any other case, the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000; where the taxation year is less than 51 weeks, paragraph 127(10.5)(b) prorates the expenditure limit for the short taxation year. As a result, the expenditure limit remains at the full $6,000,000 when prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, phases out linearly at a rate of $1.00 of expenditure limit for every $10.00 of taxable capital between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, and reaches $0 once associated taxable capital reaches or exceeds $75,000,000. Expressed directly in terms of prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada (TCprior) for a full 365-day taxation year, the linear phase-out operates as follows:

Because public corporations and capital-intensive venture-backed CCPCs frequently carry substantial paid-up capital and long-term debt on their balance sheets while generating modest commercial revenue, Bill C-15 also enacted the Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula under subsections 127(9), 127(10.6), 127(10.31) and 127(10.32). For ECPCs, the annual expenditure limit is mandatorily determined using the corporation's—or consolidated corporate group's, based on "consolidated financial statements" as defined in subsection 127(9)—average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, or over the actual one or two preceding fiscal years if the corporation has fewer than three completed fiscal years. For CCPCs, the corporation and its associated group may file an election for the taxation year to calculate its expenditure limit using this three-year average gross revenue test instead of the taxable capital employed in Canada test. Where an associated CCPC group makes this election for a taxation year, the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) ceases to apply to the group for that year.
The Basic 15% Non-Refundable Rate and Refundability Rules Under Section 127.1

Qualified SR&ED expenditures that do not qualify for the 35% enhanced rate earn the basic 15% investment tax credit under subsection 127(9). This 15% basic rate applies to qualified expenditures incurred by a qualifying CCPC or ECPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit (such as spending above the $6,000,000 cap or above a reduced phase-out limit), to corporations that are neither qualifying CCPCs nor qualifying ECPCs (including foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, large public corporations phased out by gross revenue, and large private corporations whose associated taxable capital and gross revenue exceed the $75,000,000 ceiling), and to unincorporated claimants including individuals, trusts, and partnerships.

Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act governs the conversion of unused SR&ED ITCs into cash refunds ("refundable investment tax credits"). For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs operating within their $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit, ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate on current SR&ED expenditures are 100% refundable, generating a maximum cash refund of $6,000,000 × 35% × 100% = $2,100,000 per year. By contrast, under the Bill C-15 amendments to section 127.1, ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate on restored capital expenditures and qualifying capital lease costs within the expenditure limit are 40% refundable. This provides an immediate cash refund equal to 35% × 40% = 14% of the capital expenditure, while the remaining 60% of the 35% ITC—equivalent to 21% of the capital cost—remains available as a non-refundable credit to offset Part I tax payable or be carried back or forward.

For qualifying CCPCs that are not excluded by the phase-out thresholds, ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate on current or capital expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 expenditure limit are also 40% refundable, yielding an effective 15% × 40% = 6% cash refund on excess expenditures. For large corporations, foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, and partnerships, the 15% basic ITC is 0% refundable. Because a partnership is not a taxable entity under the ITA, SR&ED expenditure deductions are claimed at the partnership level in computing partnership income, while the 15% non-refundable ITC is allocated to the individual or corporate partners under subsection 127(8). Unincorporated individuals (sole proprietors) and trusts earn the 15% basic ITC, of which 40% is refundable under section 127.1. Any non-refundable portion of a federal SR&ED ITC not deducted against Part I tax payable in the current taxation year may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years under subsection 127(9), whereas undeducted balances in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures may be carried forward indefinitely.

body.text: Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Methodologies, and Specified Employee Restrictions

To generate an investment tax credit, an outlay must first qualify for inclusion in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1)—specifically paragraph 37(1)(a) for current expenditures and paragraph 37(1)(b) for capital expenditures—and subsection 37(8), and subsequently satisfy the definition of a "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations. Furthermore, the outlay must not constitute a "prescribed expenditure" excluded under section 2902 of the Regulations, which disallows general administrative legal or accounting fees, interest and financing charges, entertainment expenses, and payments for the acquisition of rights in or arising out of SR&ED.
Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged Labour, Support Staff, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

Salaries and wages constitute the primary expenditure base of Canadian SR&ED claims. Under subsection 37(8) of the ITA and subsection 2900(2) of the ITR, eligible salary or wages—defined in subsection 248(1) as income from an office or employment under sections 5 to 8 of the ITA, inclusive of employer contributions to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Quebec Pension Plan (QPP), Employment Insurance (EI), and provincial workers' compensation boards—encompass the portion of remuneration paid to employees for the time they are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Directly engaged labour covers hands-on scientific experimentation, software coding of experimental algorithms, prototype fabrication, testing, eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, and first-line technical supervision of experimental work, whereas executive administration, human resources, finance, and commercial sales activities are excluded.

A major statutory compliance hazard for early-stage enterprises involves accrued remuneration that remains unpaid after year-end. Under subsection 78(4) (governing the subsection 37(1) income deduction) and subsection 127(26) (governing the subsection 127(9) investment tax credit), any salary, wages, or other remuneration accrued in a taxation year that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year. Instead, the expenditure is deemed to be incurred only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. Crucially, under subsection 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, although a prior-year unpaid salary that is eventually paid after the 180-day window may enter the direct SR&ED salary pool in the year of payment, it is permanently excluded from the salary base used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Consequently, deferring payroll settlement beyond 180 days post-year-end permanently forfeits the 55% overhead proxy credit on those wages.
Specified Employees: Statutory Wage Caps and Proxy Base Restrictions

To prevent owner-managers and controlling founders from inflating refundable SR&ED claims through year-end bonuses or profit distributions, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose strict statutory limits on "specified employees". Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" of a person is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—defined as a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, not less than 10% of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any other corporation that is related to the corporation, counting shares owned by persons with whom the taxpayer does not deal at arm's length—or who otherwise does not deal at arm's length with the employer.

For any individual who is a specified employee at any time during the taxation year, three cumulative statutory restrictions govern their compensation. First, all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, stock option benefits, and taxable benefits paid to a specified employee are 100% excluded from both direct SR&ED salaries and the proxy salary base. Second, under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. For the 2026 calendar year, the official CPP YMPE is $74,600.00; accordingly, the maximum direct SR&ED salary cap for one specified employee in a 2026 taxation year is 5 × $74,600.00 = $373,000.00.

Third, under subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations (and section 4.1 of the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy), the amount of a specified employee's directly engaged SR&ED salary that may be included in the salary base to earn the 55% overhead proxy is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages from the claimant in the year (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year) and 2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual:
Maximum Proxy Salary BaseSpecified Employee = min(0.75 × Total Eligible Salary, 2.5 × A × B / 365)

In this formula, A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends (A = $74,600.00 for 2026) and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual, with no proration for any portion of the year during which the employee was not yet a specified employee. For a full 365-day 2026 taxation year, the 2.5 × YMPE ceiling equals 2.5 × $74,600.00 = $186,500.00. Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, this maximum proxy limit must be allocated among the associated corporations under subsection 2900(8) of the Regulations (section 4.2 of the CRA PPA Policy).

body.text: The interplay of these dual caps is demonstrated in the comparative scenarios for the 2026 taxation year (YMPE<sub>2026</sub> = $74,600). When Founder A (owning 50% of a Calgary-based CCPC) takes a $100,000 base payroll salary and devotes 70% of their documented time to SR&ED, the $70,000 direct SR&ED salary falls below both the 75% total salary ceiling ($75,000) and the $186,500 statutory cap, allowing the full $70,000 to earn the 55% PPA ($38,500) for a total qualified expenditure of $108,500 and a federal cash refund of $37,975. Conversely, when Founder B ($100,000 salary) devotes 90% of their time to SR&ED, although the full $90,000 is allowed as direct SR&ED salary, the proxy salary base is restricted by the 75% cap under subsection 2900(7) to $75,000. Finally, for Founder C ($300,000 salary, 90% SR&ED time), the $270,000 direct SR&ED salary is allowed in full because it falls below the $373,000 (5 × YMPE) cap, but the proxy salary base is restricted to $186,500 by the 2.5 × YMPE ceiling.
Overhead Calculation Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Taxpayers must elect on Form T661 for each taxation year whether to compute SR&ED overhead using the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method; once the tax return and Form T661 are filed for a given taxation year, the chosen method is irrevocable for that year.

Under the Proxy Method, governed by subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in lieu of itemizing actual overhead costs. Since January 1, 2014 (following step-down reductions from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013, which the CRA formally purged from its updated Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy on April 28, 2022), the PPA rate has been fixed at 55% of the salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, calculated in Part 5 of Form T661. Because the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA—such as office utilities, facility maintenance, clerical support, and general supplies—are already deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a) of the ITA, the PPA itself does not enter the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool. Instead, the PPA is added directly into the definition of "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9) to earn federal and provincial investment tax credits.

Under the Traditional Method, governed by subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA, the claimant foregoes the 55% notional proxy and instead itemizes and claims actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and incremental to the carrying on of the business. While the Proxy Method is preferred by the vast majority of Canadian claimants due to its simplicity and lower audit friction, the Traditional Method remains advantageous for heavy industrial, chemical, metallurgical, or pilot-plant operations where dedicated facility power, shop supplies, and directly attributable plant overhead exceed 55% of direct technical payroll.
Materials Consumed vs. Transformed and Recapture of Investment Tax Credits

Under subsection 37(8) of the ITA and subparagraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR, the cost of materials is eligible if the materials are either consumed (destroyed, exhausted, or rendered virtually valueless during experimental trials) or transformed (physically integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom experimental assembly during the course of SR&ED).

However, when a taxpayer claims an SR&ED ITC on the cost of property—including transformed materials integrated into a prototype or eligible capital property—and subsequently sells the property or converts it to commercial use within 20 years of acquisition, subsection 127(27) (alongside subsection 127(28) for partnerships, subsection 127(29) for taxpayers that transferred qualified expenditures under an agreement, and subsection 127(34) for property acquired in non-arm's-length circumstances) triggers ITC Recapture. The recaptured amount is added directly back to the taxpayer's Part I federal tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion, calculated as the lesser of the historical SR&ED ITC earned on the property and the historical ITC percentage rate multiplied by either the proceeds of disposition (in an arm's-length sale) or the fair market value of the property at the time of conversion to commercial use.

As detailed in section 5.1 of the CRA's Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy, for recapture purposes the "cost" of a property cannot exceed the amount paid by the claimant to acquire the property from another person; it excludes internal salaries, wages, or overhead costs imputed to the fabrication or transformation of the prototype. Furthermore, where an expenditure was allowed as "cost of materials consumed" and not incorporated into an SR&ED product, no recapture occurs unless proceeds received (such as insurance proceeds or scrap value) exceed 10% of the cost of the materials. Similarly, where a payer contracts an R&D performer to conduct SR&ED and the resulting intellectual property belongs ab initio to the payer under the terms of the contract as it is generated, the payer is not acquiring property from the performer; consequently, no ITC recapture is triggered if the payer later sells, licenses, or commercializes that intellectual property.
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Transactions

Payments made to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors for SR&ED performed on behalf of the claimant in Canada are 100% deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), but only 80% of the contract expenditure enters the claimant's "qualified expenditure" pool for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9). This statutory 20% reduction strips out the subcontractor's assumed profit margin so that federal ITCs subsidize only estimated underlying R&D costs. Identical 100% deductibility and 80% qualified expenditure inclusion apply to third-party payments under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) and subsection 127(9) made to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D corporations where the claimant is entitled to exploit the research results.

By contrast, under subsection 127(9), payments made to a non-arm's-length (NAL) subcontractor for the performance of SR&ED are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures. Instead, the NAL performer must claim the qualified expenditures directly, or the NAL performer and payer may execute a joint election on Form T1146 under subsection 127(13) (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the qualified expenditures to the payer. In addition, under subsection 127(11.5) (as amended by Bill C-15 to cover restored capital property) when a claimant purchases goods, services, or capital property from a non-arm's-length supplier for SR&ED, the claimant's qualified expenditure is capped at the actual cost incurred by the NAL supplier, eliminating intercompany mark-ups.
Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Lease Costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), capital expenditures and related lease costs are restored to the SR&ED program for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and lease amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. Depreciable equipment—such as R&D laboratory and testing apparatus, prototyping machinery, specialized tools, and GPU compute clusters—intended to be used during all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualifies for 100% immediate deduction under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III), as well as 100% inclusion in qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9). Where new depreciable equipment is used primarily (more than 50%, but less than 90%) for SR&ED in Canada during its operating time, it qualifies under the restored first term shared-use-equipment and second term shared-use-equipment (SUE) provisions in subsection 127(9) and paragraph 2902(b) of the Regulations.

Chief Financial Officers and corporate tax directors acquiring capital equipment in 2025 and 2026 must model paragraph 37(1)(b) SR&ED capital claims alongside the federal accelerated capital cost allowance (CCA) measures, including the Budget 2025 Productivity Super-Deduction and the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction announced by the Department of Finance Canada on September 15, 2026, which would provide permanent immediate expensing for most depreciable property acquired on or after that date and which the Department projects would reduce Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new business investment to 6.4% compared to 16.9% in the United States. Claiming qualifying R&D hardware under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9) delivers not only a 100% immediate income deduction, but also a 35% enhanced ITC (of which 40% is refundable in cash under section 127.1 for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs) or a 15% basic ITC.

body.text: Provincial and Territorial Research and Development Tax Credit Regimes

Every Canadian province (with the exception of Prince Edward Island, which delivers innovation assistance through direct rebates) and the Yukon territory supplements the federal SR&ED program with provincial or territorial R&D tax credits. In most jurisdictions, provincial eligibility harmonizes directly with the federal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and is co-administered by the CRA through the T2 corporate income tax return, whereas Quebec and Alberta administer autonomous statutory regimes through Revenu Québec and Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, respectively.

Under paragraph 12(1)(x), paragraph 37(1)(d), and subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance". Consequently, the dollar amount of any provincial R&D tax credit earned in a taxation year reduces the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the federal qualified expenditure pool before the federal 35% or 15% ITC is computed.
Quebec: The Consolidated Research, Innovation and Commercialization Tax Credit (CRIC) and Complementary Regimes

Quebec operates the most generous provincial innovation tax system in Canada, jointly administered by Revenu Québec and Investissement Québec (IQ) under the Taxation Act (Quebec). Historically, Quebec delivered R&D support through a suite of separate refundable credits, including the Tax Credit for R&D Labour Costs (providing up to 30% on a maximum of $3,000,000 in eligible R&D salaries) and the Tax Credit for Pre-Competitive Private Partnership Research (providing up to 14% to 30% on a maximum of $3,000,000). To streamline administration and extend support beyond laboratory experimentation, the Government of Québec consolidated its legacy R&D credits into the unified Research, Innovation and Commercialization Tax Credit (CRIC). The CRIC provides a fully refundable tax credit of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures in Quebec across all corporation sizes, and 20% fully refundable on eligible expenditures exceeding $1,000,000, covering both traditional SR&ED and pre-commercialization activities such as industrial design, regulatory certification, and pilot validation.

Beyond the CRIC, Quebec enterprises can leverage four major complementary innovation incentives. First, the Development of E-Business Tax Credit Integrating Artificial Intelligence (CDAEIA), administered by Investissement Québec and Revenu Québec, provides a credit of up to 30% for IT and software corporations that integrate artificial intelligence functionalities into electronic business solutions. Second, the Investment and Innovation Tax Credit (IITC / C3i) provides a credit of up to 25% for the acquisition of manufacturing and processing equipment, computer hardware, and management software packages. Third, the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations in Québec (IDCI) functions as a provincial patent-box deduction that reduces the effective Quebec corporate income tax rate on net income derived from commercializing qualified Quebec intellectual property assets by up to 83%. Fourth, the Quebec Multimedia Titles Credit offers a refundable tax credit of up to 37.5% on eligible salaries in multimedia and video game development.
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Administered by the CRA on behalf of the Ontario Ministry of Finance, Ontario provides three stackable R&D tax credits alongside a premier digital media credit. The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) (Schedule T2SCH566) is an 8% refundable tax credit—reduced from a historical 10% rate that still appears erroneously in older practitioner guides—available to corporations on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures, yielding up to $240,000 in annual cash refunds. The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (Schedule T2SCH508) is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (net of any OITC claimed) to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Additionally, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) (Schedule T2SCH568) provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under eligible research contracts with approved Ontario post-secondary institutions or hospital research institutes, while the Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (OIDMTC), administered with Ontario Creates, provides up to a 40% refundable tax credit on qualifying labour and production costs.
British Columbia: Alignment with the $6,000,000 Federal Expenditure Limit

Under Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia), administered by the CRA via Schedule T2SCH425, the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit provides a 10% refundable tax credit for qualifying CCPCs and a 10% non-refundable tax credit for other corporations, CCPCs on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit, and active corporate members of partnerships claiming their proportionate share of the partnership's BC qualified SR&ED expenditures. Crucially, the Government of British Columbia has officially confirmed that because the BC refundable credit cannot exceed 10% of the federal expenditure limit as determined under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the federal Income Tax Act, the BC refundable SR&ED expenditure limit automatically increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, and incorporates the new federal phase-out thresholds. Consequently, a qualifying CCPC in British Columbia can now earn up to $600,000 per year (10% of $6,000,000, doubled from $300,000) in refundable provincial SR&ED credits. Separately, BC digital media studios may claim the 17.5% refundable BC Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (IDMTC) through Creative BC.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Administered autonomously by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a refundable grant/tax credit of up to 20% on up to $4,000,000 of eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta per taxation year. The IEG operates via a two-tier calculation: corporations earn an 8% base payment on all eligible Alberta R&D spending up to $4,000,000, plus a 12% incremental payment (bringing the combined rate to 20%) on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's average eligible Alberta R&D spending over the two preceding taxation years, delivering up to $800,000 per year in refundable provincial support.
Atlantic, Prairie, and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Across the Prairie and Atlantic provinces and northern territories, Manitoba offers a 15% R&D Tax Credit (partially refundable for in-house R&D and fully refundable for R&D conducted under contract with eligible educational institutions), while Saskatchewan provides a 10% R&D Tax Credit (refundable for CCPCs on the first $1,000,000 of qualifying expenditures and non-refundable on excess spending). Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit for eligible corporations with no annual expenditure cap (with Nova Scotia also offering a 50% Digital Media Tax Credit and New Brunswick offering the NBIF Innovation Voucher Fund of $10,000 to $100,000).

body.text: Interaction with Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and the Federal Innovation Grant Ecosystem

Canadian technology and manufacturing enterprises routinely stack non-dilutive direct grants, wage subsidies, and provincial tax credits with federal SR&ED investment tax credits. However, the Income Tax Act enforces strict statutory netting rules to prevent combined public subsidies from duplicating underlying project expenditures.
Statutory Mechanics of Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d), paragraph 12(1)(x), subsection 127(9) (paragraph (h) of the definition of "qualified expenditure"), and subsections 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and its SR&ED qualified expenditure pool must be reduced by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year.

Government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. As confirmed in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, this encompasses funds distributed by a non-profit organization whose funding originates from a government organization, as well as all provincial R&D tax credits. Non-government assistance covers any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance received from a private or non-governmental entity described in paragraph 12(1)(x). Contract payments are defined in subsection 127(9) as amounts paid or payable to a claimant by a "taxable supplier" (a person resident in Canada or carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada) for SR&ED performed for or on behalf of a person or partnership entitled to deduct the amount as a current expenditure or third-party payment. When the amount of assistance and contract payments relating to a project exceeds the SR&ED expenditures of the project, the qualified SR&ED expenditures of the claimant and any non-arm's-length party are reduced to nil under subsection 127(19). Conversely, when a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its qualified expenditures, paragraph 37(1)(c) adds the repaid amount back into the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the year of repayment, and subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8) restore the corresponding ITC.
The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Stacking Asymmetry: Why NRC IRAP and SR&ED Amplify Returns

A crucial technical asymmetry in the Income Tax Regulations makes stacking direct wage grants—most notably the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—with the federal SR&ED Proxy Method highly advantageous. When NRC IRAP reimburses a CCPC for 80% of direct internal R&D salaries, that non-repayable contribution constitutes "government assistance" that reduces the total SR&ED qualified expenditure pool on Part 4 of Form T661 under subsection 127(18). However, under section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, government assistance does NOT reduce the salary base on Part 5 of Form T661 used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Consequently, the claimant earns the 55% notional overhead proxy on 100% of the eligible direct SR&ED salaries—including the 80% salary portion reimbursed by NRC IRAP—before the IRAP grant is deducted from the combined pool of direct salaries, eligible materials, and proxy overhead.

body.text: As demonstrated in the quantitative model above, when an Ontario CCPC incurs $500,000 in direct SR&ED salaries and $50,000 in materials ($550,000 total cash outlay) and receives an 80% NRC IRAP grant ($400,000), it claims SR&ED on the $100,000 of salaries it paid itself, the $50,000 in materials, and the full $275,000 overhead proxy (55% of $500,000) that IRAP did not fund. After netting the $400,000 IRAP grant, $34,000 Ontario OITC refund, and $13,685 Ontario ORDTC credit, the remaining $377,315 federal pool generates a $132,060.25 federal SR&ED refund—resulting in $579,745.25 in combined non-dilutive recovery on $550,000 of cash R&D expenditure.
Restructuring of the Federal Direct Innovation Funding Landscape (2025–2026)

Taxpayers coordinating prospective grant applications with retrospective SR&ED claims must navigate four major structural changes across federal innovation programs executed in 2025 and 2026. First, NRC IRAP remains Canada's flagship SME innovation program—funding projects across Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) 3 to 7 with a $75,000 median non-repayable contribution and awards reaching up to $1,000,000—and has officially absorbed Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC). SDTC was wound into the National Research Council and no longer operates a standalone intake; clean-technology innovators now apply directly through NRC IRAP Clean Technology.

Second, the former Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) was restructured and renamed the Strategic Response Fund (SRF) under Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED). The SRF is not an SME grant program: it imposes a $10,000,000 minimum contribution threshold, requires a mandatory consultation before submitting a statement of interest, and is structured as a repayable contribution rather than a grant. Third, Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC) experienced a budget reduction of $70,000,000 per year beginning in 2025–2026, though its Challenge and Testing streams remain operational alongside the Department of National Defence's IDEaS (Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security) program, which provides up to $1,500,000 for defence and dual-use R&D. Fourth, while the Canada Digital Adoption Program (CDAP) wound down in 2025 and was permanently discontinued without a federal micro-grant replacement, the federal government launched its national artificial intelligence strategy, AI for All, on June 4, 2026, complemented by the NRC AI for Productivity Challenge ($250,000 to $2,000,000 collaborative R&D agreements running to 2033), the ISED AI Compute Challenge, and the Scale AI Supercluster (offering up to $50,000 for acceleration projects alongside supply-chain AI investments).
Administrative Governance, Filing Mechanics, and Audit Defence Protocols
Mandatory Tax Forms, Part 2 Technical Narratives, and Claim Preparer Penalties

To claim federal SR&ED deductions and investment tax credits, a claimant must file a complete prescribed form package with the CRA. Every claimant must submit Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), which is organized into five core functional parts (plus summary, checklist, certification, and claim preparer disclosure sections): Part 1 captures general corporate identification; Part 2 contains project-by-project technical descriptions; Part 3 calculates the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and records the proxy versus traditional overhead election; Part 4 calculates the subsection 127(9) pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures net of assistance and contract payments; and Part 5 computes the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount and enforces the specified employee salary base caps. Corporate claimants must also file Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) alongside their T2 return, Schedule T2SCH49 where associated CCPCs allocate the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, and Form T1146 for non-arm's-length expenditure transfers.

In Part 2 of Form T661, claimants must submit a separate project description for each SR&ED project claimed—or may elect at the time of filing to submit Part 2 for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, subject to the CRA's authority to demand Part 2 descriptions for any or all remaining projects during review. Failure to provide Part 2 information results in mandatory disallowance of the project's expenditures. Section B of Part 2 enforces strict word limits across three mandatory technical prompts that mirror the CRA's eligibility criteria:

cells: What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome?

Must articulate the specific scientific knowledge gap or system-level technological limitation that could not be resolved using standard practice or publicly available engineering routines. Must distinguish technological uncertainty from commercial or business objectives.
What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the technological obstacles/uncertainties described in Line 242?

Must chronicle the systematic investigation executed during the specific fiscal year: the explicit hypotheses formulated, the controlled experiments or analyses performed, quantitative parameters tested, iterative modifications after failed runs, and logical conclusions.
What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244?

Must state the new scientific or technological knowledge generated—quantifying performance metrics achieved or explaining the scientific reasons discovered for why a tested hypothesis failed—and linking the new knowledge directly back to the uncertainty in Line 242.

body.text: The Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 containing all prescribed information in respect of an expenditure on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the statutory deadline for a corporation to file an SR&ED claim is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year:
Corporate SR&ED Statutory Deadline = Taxation Year-End + 6 Months (T2 Filing-Due Date) + 12 Months

This 18-month filing deadline is an absolute statutory bar. As illustrated in Tax Court litigation such as 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC), if a taxpayer fails to file the prescribed forms and prescribed project and expenditure information within the 18-month window prescribed by subsection 37(11) and subsection 127(9)(m), the claim is statutorily barred and neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada has discretion to waive the deadline.
CRA Review Procedures, AI Screening, and the April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process

Across the national program, CRA operational statistics confirm that 90% of SR&ED claims are accepted as filed, 6% are accepted after financial or technical changes, and 4% are denied. As part of its administrative modernization introduced in 2025 and 2026, the CRA has deployed AI-supported claim screening to triage low-risk claims for rapid automated processing while directing audit resources toward high-risk filings. Most significantly, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a new elective pre-claim approval process. For claims that undergo this upfront pre-claim approval process and subsequently require an expenditure review after filing, the CRA's processing timeframe is cut in half from 180 days to 90 days, providing substantially faster cash-flow certainty for R&D-intensive enterprises.

When a claim is selected for technical and financial audit, the CRA assigns a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) to evaluate scientific eligibility under subsection 248(1) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) to verify expenditure substantiation, employee time-tracking records by project, contractor invoices, and associated-corporation allocations. Every dollar claimed must be tied to a specific project, a specific employee or vendor, and a specific date through contemporaneous project-level time tracking and experimental documentation.

If the Minister issues a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment disallowing an SR&ED claim, the taxpayer may challenge the decision by serving a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days of the Notice of Assessment. Under paragraph 166.2(5)(a) of the Income Tax Act, any application to extend the time to file a Notice of Objection must be made within a strict statutory window of one year and 90 days after the assessment date; as the Tax Court confirmed in Odebala-Fregene (2015 DTC 1087), common-law principles of procedural fairness or discoverability cannot override this strict statutory deadline. Following an unfavourable decision by the CRA Appeals Division (or if 90 days elapse without a decision), the taxpayer may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada under section 169 of the ITA—where 65% to 70% of SR&ED appeals proceed under the streamlined Informal Procedure and larger claims proceed under the formal General Procedure—and from there on questions of law to the Federal Court of Appeal.
Strategic Conclusions and Tax Planning Imperatives

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, fundamentally reshapes the economics of conducting research and development in Canada for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. By doubling the enhanced 35% expenditure limit to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $2,100,000 in annual federal cash refunds and automatically doubling British Columbia's refundable CCPC cap to $600,000), expanding the taxable capital phase-out corridor to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, introducing an elective three-year gross revenue phase-out calculation, extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, and restoring capital property and lease costs under paragraph 37(1)(b) and section 127.1, Parliament has established the most generous statutory R&D regime in Canadian history.

To capture the full value of these reforms while insulating claims against audit disallowance, corporate tax executives and engineering leaders must execute four coordinated compliance practices. First, CFOs of scaling CCPCs and public innovators must annually model both the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital test and the three-year average consolidated gross revenue election across all associated entities to maximize access to the $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit. Second, hardware, AI, cleantech, and manufacturing firms acquiring GPUs, laboratory equipment, or prototyping machinery on or after December 16, 2024, must evaluate claiming those assets under restored paragraph 37(1)(b) rather than ordinary CCA or the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction to capture the 35% enhanced ITC and 40% capital refundability under section 127.1. Third, enterprises utilizing specified employees (10%+ shareholders) must structure compensation through regular base payroll remitted within 180 days of year-end—avoiding bonuses and monitoring the $186,500 (2.5 × YMPE) and 75% proxy base caps—while strategically stacking NRC IRAP wage grants with the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount to preserve notional overhead credits on grant-funded payroll. Finally, R&D teams must embed contemporaneous hypothesis-and-test tracking directly into engineering workflows from project inception and leverage the CRA's April 1, 2026 elective pre-claim approval process to halve expenditure review timelines to 90 days.
